question: What is the primary difference between LiveKit client SDKs and server SDKs?
options: Client SDKs can only publish tracks while server SDKs can only subscribe to tracks
Client SDKs are written in JavaScript while server SDKs are written in Python
Server SDKs are faster because they run on more powerful hardware
Client SDKs connect end-user devices to rooms, while server SDKs handle backend operations like token generation, room management, and webhooks
explanation: Client SDKs connect end-user devices (browsers, mobile apps, desktops) to LiveKit rooms — they implement Room, Participant, and Track abstractions for each platform. Server SDKs run on your backend and handle operations that should never happen on a client: generating access tokens with specific grants, creating and managing rooms, ejecting participants, starting egress, and processing webhooks. They mirror the three roles in a LiveKit application.

question: Why does LiveKit provide a consistent API across all client SDKs on different platforms?
options: So that learning LiveKit once lets developers build everywhere — the mental model of rooms, participants, and tracks is identical regardless of platform
To reduce code size by sharing identical implementations across platforms
Because all platforms use the same programming language under the hood
Because WebRTC requires identical APIs on every platform
explanation: Every client SDK exposes the same conceptual API: connecting to a room, subscribing to tracks, publishing media, and handling participant events work the same way whether you are writing TypeScript for the web, Swift for iOS, or Kotlin for Android. This consistency means a developer who built a LiveKit web app can contribute to the mobile app without learning a new conceptual framework. Method names adapt to platform conventions, but the mental model is identical.
